title: Latency path signature lab notes
content:
Overview:

This is a working note from the signature-clustering exercise run on the e2e trace corpus (Nov 2025 snapshot). Goal: identify the small set of 'path signatures' that explain the majority of p95/p99 tail when serving the text-generation workload on dedicated-gpu pools. This doc captures how we sliced traces, the stage mappings we used, aggregate percentiles, representative trace examples, and a short troubleshooting checklist for follow-ups.

Why 'path signature'?:
- Traditional per-stage p95/p99 looks at stage durations independently. Path signature = ordered vector of stage presences + stage-duration quantiles for a single trace. Clustering these gives us common end-to-end execution shapes (e.g., kernel-heavy with cold KV misses, or decode-heavy with long postprocess).

Experiment setup:
- Trace corpus: 120k e2e traces collected across two dedicated clusters (cluster-a, cluster-b) over 72 hours (2025-10-28 to 2025-10-31).
- Sampling filter: only traces with total duration > 150ms (to focus on tails). Final set = 18,900 traces.
- Instrumentation: rtrace v0.7.3 with stage tags: inbound-parse, route-lookup, auth, kv-lookup, model-load, kernel-exec, decode, postprocess, response-encode, outbound.
- Offline tools: trace-fingerprint -> compute signature vector, signature-cluster k=6 (silhouette peak at k=6).
- Environment: g4dn-equivalent nodes; model=manticore-7b-int8, batch config default (auto-batch, max-batch=8), KV cache TTL=60s.

Aggregate percentiles (all selected traces):
- e2e p50: 41ms
- e2e p95: 178ms
- e2e p99: 517ms

Top 6 path signatures (short descriptions):
1) Kernel-bound short-io (33% of tail traces)
   - signature: kernel-exec dominant (p95 kernel=120ms), kv-lookup ~5ms, decode~10ms
   - likely cause: long attention ops on dense seqlen > 1024; GPU kernel scheduling contention at high QPS
2) KV-miss coldstart (22%)
   - signature: kv-lookup spike (p95 kv=230ms), followed by model-load 80ms (local fallback), small kernel time thereafter
   - likely cause: prefix cache miss and on-demand fetch from external Redis-like store; sometimes serialized network blips
3) Decode-heavy long-token outputs (14%)
   - signature: decode dominates (p95 decode=275ms), kernel smaller; correlated with long generation sequences (>256 tokens)
4) Postprocess backpressure (9%)
   - signature: postprocess and response-encode large (p95 post=160ms), often when output has heavy JSON serialization and function-calling parsing
5) Route lookup + auth thrash (12%)
   - signature: route-lookup and auth total ~120ms; kernel minimal; mapped to complex policy checks and external OPA calls
6) Mixed micro-latency pileups (10%)
   - signature: multiple stages small but additive (many ~20-40ms), total reaching p99; no single dominant stage.

Representative trace excerpts (anonymized):
- Trace A (Kernel-bound short-io):
  events: inbound-parse 2ms -> route-lookup 3ms -> kv-lookup 6ms -> kernel-exec 132ms -> decode 12ms -> postprocess 4ms -> outbound 2ms
  total: 161ms

- Trace B (KV-miss coldstart):
  events: inbound-parse 3ms -> route-lookup 4ms -> kv-lookup 245ms (remote GET timeout 150ms then fallback) -> model-load 78ms -> kernel-exec 14ms -> decode 6ms -> outbound 2ms
  total: 352ms

Hypotheses and short tests run so far:
- H1: Majority of kv-miss spikes are due to remote-GET 1) network path and 2) serialization cost on the Redis client. Quick test: instrumented client shows average remote-get serialization 32ms; network median 18ms; but in spikes network was 140–200ms during a narrow window.
- H2: Kernel-bound traces correlate with 90th-percentile seqlen. We computed seqlen distribution: 90p seqlen for tail cluster=1248 vs corpus median 384. Suggests kernel scheduling + attention matmul cost.
- H3: Postprocess spikes are caused by certain prompt types that trigger heavy tool-calling parsing (structured JSON). Confirmed by correlating prompt template id -> postprocess time (template T-119 has median postprocess 110ms in tail).

Quick repro checklist (for SRE/infra follow-up):
- Reproduce kernel-bound case: run rperf run --seqlen=1280 --batch=1 against cluster-a pods during low-noise window. Compare gpu-util & kernel-latency logs.
- Reproduce kv-miss: run trace-replay for traces with kv-lookup > 150ms against a staging Redis instance routed through the same VPC path. Enable tcpdump for 30s.
- Isolate postprocess: create synthetic request using template T-119, measure postprocess only via trace-probe v0.9 to confirm 1) CPU vs 2) blocking IO (http calls).

Suggested mitigations (short list):
- KV: enable local read-through cache for hot prefixes + increase pipeline parallelism for remote GETs (async IO). Also add client-side 100ms conservative timeout to avoid blocking model inference pipeline.
- Kernel: introduce seqlen-aware routing (route long-seq requests to lower-concurrency GPU lanes with reserved batches) and try optimized kernels (PR #4621 experiments).
- Postprocess: move heavy JSON parsing to a worker thread pool, limit synchronous tool calls in the hot path.

Next actions / owners:
- Priya: run rperf reproductions and attach kernel flame traces (target date: 2026-02-24).
- Diego: spin up Redis staging with identical VPC path, run trace-replay and tcpdump (target date: 2026-02-21).
- Evan: prototype seqlen-aware router rule (draft branch: feat/seqlen-router) and coordinate canary (target date: 2026-03-01).

Open questions and notes to self:
- How much of the kernel-bound tail is mitigatable by quantization vs scheduling? Need cost vs latency tradeoff runbook.
- Consider increasing the trace sampling for mid-range latency (50-200ms) to better understand mixed pileups. Current corpus undersamples that band.

Commands and snippets used:
- Collecting traces: rtrace collect --tag-serving --duration 72h --out traces-2025-10-28-31.json
- Fingerprint + cluster: trace-fingerprint traces-*.json | signature-cluster --k 6 --out clusters.csv
- Replay: trace-replay --input sample.json --target staging-redis --tcpdump /tmp/replay.pcap

Attachments / artifacts:
- clusters.csv (attached to INF-2384)
- sample-trace-A.json (in artifact bucket, id: s3://redwood-playback/trace-samples/2025-10/a.json)

If you want a quick visual: I produced a 2-panel view (histogram of per-stage durations + stacked timeline sample) in the notebook (not committed yet). Ask Priya for the notebook link if needed; she has the visualization paired with the clustering UMAP.

-- Evan
